---
created: 2026-06-26T00:00:00.000Z
title: Revoke shares on rename/replace-over-existing-destination (web + desktop)
area: fuse
severity: high
source: PR #568 adversarial review (revocation-completeness lens) — 2026-06-26
files:
  - crates/fuse/src/write_ops/implementation/rename.rs
  - crates/fuse/src/platform/windows/write_ops.rs
  - packages/sdk/src/bin/index.ts
  - packages/sdk/src/client.ts
  - apps/api/src/shares/shares.controller.ts
---

## Problem

PRs #563 (web/SDK) and #568 (desktop FUSE) added fail-closed share revocation on
**delete** — but only on the delete-to-bin path. When a file/folder is **renamed
or moved OVER an existing destination** (replace/overwrite), the destination node
is destroyed WITHOUT revoking its shares. This is the same data-exposure class as
the delete bug those PRs closed: the destination's `Share` / `ShareInvite` rows
stay active against content that has been replaced (and, on the unix file branch,
its CID is even unpinned), so sharees retain read access to vanished content.

Confirmed by the #568 completeness review as **pre-existing on every surface**:

- **Unix FUSE:** `crates/fuse/src/write_ops/implementation/rename.rs` (~163-186) —
  the File branch destroys the dest node and even spawns `unpin_content` on the
  dest CID, with no share revocation.
- **Windows FUSE:** `crates/fuse/src/platform/windows/write_ops.rs` (~1097-1124) —
  same replace-over-dest path, no revocation.
- **Web / SDK:** the #563 revocation (`revokeSharesForItemsFn`) is wired ONLY into
  `addToBin` (`packages/sdk/src/bin/index.ts:483`, `client.ts:221`), NOT into any
  overwrite/replace/move path.

So there is NO web-vs-desktop parity regression — it's an equal gap on both, and
#568 correctly scoped rename out (delete-only).

## Solution

When a rename/move overwrites an existing destination, revoke the **destination
node's** shares before/as the destination is destroyed, mirroring the delete-path
fail-closed contract (`POST /shares/revoke-for-items`, revoke-before-destructive-
mutation, abort on failure where the call site allows it):

1. **Web/SDK:** wire revocation into the replace/overwrite path (whatever the SDK
   uses when a move/upload clobbers an existing destination), reusing the existing
   `revokeSharesForItems` helper + chunking + 4xx short-circuit.
2. **Unix FUSE** (`rename.rs`): revoke the dest node's `ipnsName`
   (`file_meta_ipns_name` for a file dest) before destroying it; reuse
   `metadata::revoke_shares_blocking` (added in #568). Fail-closed via `EIO` if the
   handler return path allows it.
3. **Windows FUSE** (`write_ops.rs`): same, at the corresponding replace point.

Clarify dest-can-be-a-folder semantics: POSIX `rename` over a non-empty dir fails,
but check the app's move/replace semantics — if a folder dest is reachable, decide
whether a subtree walk is needed (delete used the bottom-up invariant; replace may
not have it).

Tests: web-e2e + desktop-e2e that a shared file replaced via move/overwrite revokes
its share, plus unit coverage. Depends on the live `/shares/revoke-for-items`
endpoint (already shipped in #563).

# Share/Key Data Model: Report

The user's "only the root needs to be in DB" model is **refuted**. Here is the evidence, by sub-question.

## 1. `share_keys` schema — one row PER ITEM, not per root
`share-key.entity.ts:14-51`: columns are `id` (uuid PK), `share_id` (FK→shares, CASCADE, `share-key.entity.ts:21-26`), `key_type` varchar(12) (`share-key.entity.ts:32-33`), `item_id` varchar(255) (`share-key.entity.ts:38-40`), `encrypted_key` bytea (`share-key.entity.ts:46-47`), `created_at`. Unique on `(shareId, keyType, itemId)` (`share-key.entity.ts:15`). `keyType` ∈ `['file','folder','file-ipns','folder-ipns']` (`types.ts:15-20`); `itemId` = the file/subfolder UUID; `encryptedKey` = that item's key **ECIES-wrapped to the RECIPIENT's pubkey** (`share-key.entity.ts:42-47`). Verdict: **one row per descendant item per share** (plus per IPNS key) — the root's own key lives separately on `shares.encrypted_key` (`share.entity.ts:61-67`).

## 2. Does folderKey-chaining recover all child keys? NO
`METADATA_SCHEMAS.md:140-147`: `FolderEntry.folderKeyEncrypted` and `ipnsPrivateKeyEncrypted` are **ECIES-wrapped to the vault OWNER's secp256k1 publicKey** — "encrypted to the vault owner's public key." The FolderMetadata *blob* is AES-GCM under `folderKey` (`METADATA_SCHEMAS.md:46,93`), so a recipient with the folderKey can *read* the blob and *see* the wrapped child ciphertext — but cannot ECIES-unwrap it (lacks the owner's privateKey). Same for `FileMetadata.fileKeyEncrypted` (`METADATA_SCHEMAS.md:199,208`). Verdict: **folderKey alone does NOT yield descendant keys** — they are sealed to the owner, not derivable.

## 3. Write IPNS private key — from `share_keys`/`shares`, NOT metadata
Root node's IPNS key: `shares.encrypted_ipns_key`, wrapped for recipient (`share.entity.ts:76-82`; `shares.service.ts:84-91`). Descendant IPNS keys: `share_keys` rows with `keyType` `folder-ipns`/`file-ipns` (`shared-write.ts:319-323`, `309-324`). Recipient navigation unwraps these with their own key (sub-agent: `useSharedNavigationActions.ts:282-296`, `121-130`). The owner-wrapped `FolderEntry.ipnsPrivateKeyEncrypted` is re-wrapped for the recipient at share time (`key-wrapping.ts:112-125`, `ShareDialog.tsx:248-258`). Verdict: **from DB, ECIES-wrapped to recipient.**

## 4. Selective/deep share WITHOUT parent? YES
A share anchors to a single `ipnsName` (`SHARING.md:22`; `share.entity.ts:42-43`). `createShare` stores that node's key on `shares.encrypted_key` and recurses *from that node down* via `collectChildKeys` (`ShareDialog.tsx:233-278`, `key-wrapping.ts:38-164`); files share the parent folderKey + fileKey (`ShareDialog.tsx:283-304`). Verdict: **yes — any node (deep subfolder or single file) can be a share root**, unreachable by chaining from the vault root, which independently necessitates storing its key in DB.

## 5. Why `reWrapForRecipients`/`addShareKeys` per new item? Because chaining can't deliver the key
`reWrapForRecipients` wraps each new child key for each recipient and writes `share_keys` (`index.ts:88-134`; `shared-write.ts:213-223`, `309-324`). This is required precisely because the updated FolderMetadata embeds the new child's key wrapped **to the owner** (sub-question 2) — a recipient parsing it cannot decrypt it. The per-item DB row provides: the read key (`folder`/`file`) re-wrapped to the recipient, AND the IPNS write key (`folder-ipns`/`file-ipns`). Verdict: **metadata-chaining provides nothing decryptable to a recipient; the DB row is the only channel.**

## 6. Revocation granularity
Revoke = soft-delete `shares.revoked_at` (`shares.service.ts:258-271`); rows kept for lazy folderKey rotation. Hard-delete (`completeRotation`, `revokeForItems`) removes the `Share` and **CASCADE-deletes all its `share_keys`** (`share.entity.ts:24`, `98`; `shares.service.ts:401-402`, `304-314`). Permission downgrade deletes only `file-ipns`/`folder-ipns` rows in a txn (`shares.service.ts:489-494`) — finer than whole-share. Verdict: **per-item rows enable selective revocation of write keys (downgrade) without dropping read access; full revoke cascades all.**

## Synthesis
The "only the root in DB" model is **not viable**. The decisive reason is the **read-key embedding gap**: every child key inside FolderMetadata/FileMetadata is ECIES-sealed to the *owner's* pubkey (`METADATA_SCHEMAS.md:140-147,199`), so a recipient holding only the folderKey can decrypt the metadata blob but not the owner-wrapped child keys within it — they must receive each child key re-wrapped to *their* pubkey, which is exactly what `share_keys` stores. Three further factors reinforce per-item rows: **IPNS write-key distribution** (write recipients need each node's signing key, sealed to the owner in metadata — sub-question 3), **selective deep shares** (a share root may be any node, so its key cannot be chained from the vault root — sub-question 4), and **revocation granularity** (per-key-type deletion lets a write→read downgrade strip IPNS keys while preserving read access — sub-question 6). One ambiguity worth noting: the design *could* theoretically have wrapped descendant keys to the recipient inline in a recipient-specific metadata copy, but CipherBox deliberately keeps a single owner-wrapped metadata tree and offloads recipient re-wrapping to the DB.

## 1. The rename-replace todo — you've read it as the wrong node

Your mental model is **correct**, but for a *different* scenario than the todo targets. There are two cases, and the todo is only about the second:

**Case A — move a shared item around the vault (no name collision).** Exactly as you described: source folder drops the child, dest folder's metadata gains it, the item keeps its own `ipnsName` + keys. In `rename.rs` this is the re-parent path (lines 196–226) plus, for cross-folder moves, a re-encrypt of the file's `FileMetadata` to the new folderKey (lines 247–259). The share **survives** — and not because the grant lives in the file metadata, but because (a) the `Share` row is keyed by the node's `ipnsName`, which doesn't change on a move, and (b) the sharee holds the `fileKey` directly. **The todo does not touch this path. You're right that it should stay active.**

**Case B — rename/move A *over an existing* B (overwrite).** This is the todo's actual target — the title's "replace-over-existing-destination." Here **B, the destination, is destroyed**: `rename.rs:172–186` spawns `unpin_content` on B's CID and removes B's inode. If B was shared, B's `Share`/`ShareInvite` rows stay live against content that's been clobbered and unpinned — an orphaned grant, same data-exposure class as the delete bug #563/#568 just closed. The todo proposes revoking **B's** shares (the clobbered destination), never A's (the thing you moved).

So the todo is valid; it just isn't about "moving a shared file revokes its share." It's "overwriting a shared file by renaming another onto it leaves the victim's share dangling." It's also **low-frequency** in practice (you'd have to rename one file onto another, specifically-shared, file) — I'd keep it but consider dropping severity from `high` → `medium`, or folding it into a general "revoke on any node destruction" sweep rather than its own phase. Want me to tighten the todo's wording (it currently invites exactly the misread you had) while you're on this docs branch?

> Side note that bridges to Q2: your "share details are stored in the file IPFS metadata AFAIK" is the part that's off. The *grant* (recipient + their wrapped keys) lives in the DB, not the metadata — which is the whole of Q2.

---

## 2. Why per-item key material lives in `share_keys` (not just the root)

Short answer: **your "chain down from the root folderKey" model would work only if folder metadata sealed each child under the parent folderKey. It deliberately doesn't — it seals every child key to the *owner's* identity key.** So chaining yields nothing decryptable for a recipient.

Walk through what a recipient holding just the root folderKey can actually do:

1. The FolderMetadata **blob** is AES-GCM under `folderKey`, so they *can* decrypt the blob and **see** the child entries.
2. But inside, each child's `folderKeyEncrypted` / `fileKeyEncrypted` / `ipnsPrivateKeyEncrypted` is **ECIES-wrapped to the vault owner's secp256k1 pubkey** (`METADATA_SCHEMAS.md:140-147,199`) — *not* under the folderKey. The recipient lacks the owner's private key, so they **cannot unwrap a single child key.** The chain dead-ends at the first descendant.

That's the **read-key embedding gap**, and it's the decisive reason. Each child key must be *re-wrapped to the recipient's* pubkey — which is precisely what a `share_keys` row is (`encrypted_key` = item key ECIES-wrapped to the recipient; one row per `(share, keyType, itemId)`).

Three reinforcing reasons the rows have to exist:

- **Write access = IPNS private keys.** To publish an updated metadata record, a writer needs each node's IPNS *private* key. Those are also owner-sealed in metadata, so they're re-wrapped per recipient as `share_keys` rows with `keyType` `file-ipns` / `folder-ipns` (root's is on `shares.encrypted_ipns_key`). Your parenthetical — "including the ipns keys… for write permissions" — is exactly this; but they can't be recovered from metadata, they have to be re-wrapped into the DB.
- **Selective / deep shares.** A share can be anchored at *any* node — a deep subfolder or a lone file — not just the vault root. Such a node isn't reachable by chaining from the root at all, so its key must be stored directly. `share_keys` is the general carrier.
- **Revocation granularity.** Per-`(item, keyType)` rows let a **write→read downgrade** delete just the `*-ipns` rows (strip write, keep read) in a txn (`shares.service.ts:489-494`); a full revoke CASCADE-deletes all of them. A single root key couldn't express "revoke write but keep read."

**Honest caveat:** this is a *consequence of a design choice*, not an iron law. CipherBox keeps **one canonical owner-wrapped metadata tree** and offloads per-recipient re-wrapping to the DB. The alternative — embedding recipient-specific wrapped keys inline (a per-recipient metadata copy) — would avoid the DB rows but fork the metadata tree per recipient and complicate publishing. Given the single-tree choice, "only the root in DB" isn't viable; the `share_keys` rows are how recipients get keys the owner-sealed metadata won't give them.

This is also *why* the rename-overwrite case (Q1) is a real leak: those `share_keys` rows for the clobbered B persist with no node behind them until something revokes them.

> AGENT

Real concern, and a sharp one. You've spotted that the current design is **O(items × recipients)** in stored key material — sealing each child key to the *owner's* identity key is exactly what forces per-item re-wrapping per recipient. 1000×1000 folders/files × 10 users = 10M `share_keys` rows, and every revoke cascades all of them.

Your instinct — drive it from metadata via key *chaining* so one wrapped root key per recipient unlocks the subtree — is the right axis to attack. But there are non-obvious traps (read-only must not leak the IPNS write key; revocation shifts from a cheap DB cascade to potentially-expensive key rotation + IPNS republishing; naive "embed per-recipient keys in metadata" just relocates the 10M blowup and adds republish storms). Since this is crypto with no migration safety net, I'll run a design workflow: several independent redesigns, each adversarially reviewed for zero-knowledge / read-write leakage / revocation cost, then synthesized into one concrete recommendation.

Basically, having all these keys in the database is a sidechain on the shared folder contents - a very blurry sidechain, but one none the less.

> AGENT

Exactly right, and that framing is worth making precise because it's the strongest argument for the rework:

`share_keys` is a **denormalized projection of the folder tree** — one row per node, but flattened (it drops the parent/child edges the metadata tree already encodes) and re-keyed per recipient. It's a *second source of truth* for access control that application code has to keep reconciled with the real tree on every mutation: `reWrapForRecipients` on add, CASCADE on revoke, delete `*-ipns` rows on downgrade.

And "blurry" is the right word, because that reconciliation is manual and lossy — which is **precisely why we keep finding revocation-gap todos.** The delete-bypass (#563/#568) and the rename-overwrite-bypass are the same defect: a mutation path that touched the tree but forgot to poke the sidechain, leaving a grant pointing at a node that's gone. Fold the keys *into* the tree (chaining/derivation) and that whole bug class disappears — destroying a node intrinsically destroys access, because the key flows from the structure, not a shadow copy.

The honest counter (the skeptic lens in the workflow): you don't *delete* the consistency problem, you **move** it. Today's risk is "DB sidechain desyncs from tree on mutation." The metadata-driven risk is "revoke = rotate + re-seal + re-publish N IPNS records, and a partial failure leaves the tree half-rotated." The mainchain becomes the IPNS-published tree, and revocation becomes a tree-rewrite that has to be near-atomic. That's the trade the workflow is costing out right now — cheaper, self-consistent shares vs. heavier, must-not-half-fail revokes.

But the fix is **not** a key hierarchy (A/B) — those make the worst operation catastrophic. The fix is a **lockbox envelope (C)** that decouples grant-count from item-count while keeping node keys independent and DB-anchored.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Recommended design: Lockbox for read/write key distribution + DB-anchored shares + unchanged independent node keys\n\n**Adopt Proposal C (per-share lockbox), corrected for the blockers its reviews surfaced, and explicitly reject A and B.** This is a hybrid in one precise sense: **key *distribution* moves into a lockbox object; key *ownership/independence* and *share anchoring/authorization* stay in the DB and the existing per-node random-key model.** Nothing moves into `FolderMetadata`.\n\nWhy C over the alternatives, grounded in the reviews:\n\n| Property | A (chaining) | B (HKDF) | C (lockbox) | D (lazy DB) |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| share-create | O(recipients) ✅ | O(recipients) ✅ | **O(items) seal once + O(recipients)** ✅ | O(recipients) but needs unbuilt owner-online protocol ⚠️ |\n| add-item | O(1) ✅ | O(1) ✅ | **O(shares-covering-node)** ✅ | deferred, owner-online-coupled ⚠️ |\n| revoke (real) | O(subtree) reseal+**republish** ❌ | O(subtree) **republish storm** ❌ | **O(items) node-rotate, recipient-facing O(recipients)** ✅ | O(items) — same storm, was hidden ❌ |\n| write→read downgrade | unsound O(1) claim ❌ | O(subtree) republish ❌ | **O(1) drop write shareKey** ✅ | O(rows) delete, cached-key hole ⚠️ |\n| move-node | O(1) ✅ | reintroduces O(items×recip) via `keyWrap` ❌ | **O(1), keys sealed by stable itemId** ✅ | O(1) ✅ |\n| navigate | O(depth) unseal ✅ | O(depth) HKDF ✅ | **O(1) after one lockbox fetch** ✅ | O(depth) + owner round-trip ❌ |\n| Revocation containment | whole-subtree only ❌ | whole-subtree only ❌ | **per-node independent keys** ✅ | per-node independent ✅ |\n| New crypto primitives | needs AAD on seal | needs content-key fix + IPNS decoupling | **needs AAD/HKDF domain-sep + signed lockbox** | none |\n\nC wins because it is the **only** design that simultaneously (a) decouples grant storage from item count, (b) keeps node keys independent so revocation is *containable* and downgrade is genuinely O(1), and (c) leaves moves R-independent. A and B fail (b) and (c) structurally; D fails (a) without building a new owner-online protocol and re-incurs full cost for whole-tree (FUSE) recipients.\n\n### The mandatory corrections (these are not optional — they came up as BLOCKERs in C's reviews and apply identically wherever relevant)\n\n**C1 — Seal the key that actually gates reads.** All three C reviews independently found the schema's fatal flaw: `FileMetadata` is AES-GCM sealed under the **parent `folderKey`**, and the inner `fileKey` is the *content* key. Sealing `fileKey` alone in the lockbox grants nothing — the recipient also needs the `folderKey` to unseal `FileMetadata` (to even get the `cid`/`fileIv`). **Fix (clean break, allowed by constraint 7): re-architect `FileMetadata` to self-encrypt under its own `fileKey`** so a file is a first-class shareable node. Then the lockbox sealing `fileKey` genuinely grants single-file read access, and per-file selective revocation becomes possible. This is the load-bearing schema change and the reason a clean break is worth doing.\n\n**C2 — Write revocation requires Ed25519 IPNS keypair rotation, not just shareKey re-seal.** Verified across reviews (`ipns.service.ts`: \"authorization is by ipnsName, not by user, so any holder of the key may publish\"). Re-sealing the write lockbox does nothing to a cached IPNS private key. **Real write-revoke = generate new Ed25519 keypair → new k51 name → rewrite parent pointer → republish.** This breaks the \"itemId is stable\" assumption *for write revocation specifically* and must be costed honestly (see §4).\n\n**C3 — Bind every sealed entry with AEAD AAD = `domain-tag | itemId | keyType | generation`.** Without it, a malicious server can transplant a sealed blob between entries (e.g., move a folder key into a file slot) and the client unseals it under the same `shareKey` and binds the wrong key to the wrong node. `sealAesGcm` currently exposes no AAD parameter — **this is a new primitive requirement.** (Alternatively derive a per-entry key via the already-present `deriveContextKey(shareKey, \\`${itemId}:${keyType}:${generation}\\`)` — HKDF is present, contradicting C's \"not needed\" claim.)\n\n**C4 — Sign the lockbox; make `generation` monotonic and verified.** `lockbox_generation` as a plaintext server-side int is advisory only — a recipient can resolve a stale/old CID directly from IPFS and the server cannot enforce a floor. **The lockbox body must carry a sharer-Ed25519 signature over `{generation, root, merkle-root-of-entries}`; recipients reject non-monotonic generations and unsigned/mismatched bodies.**\n\n**C5 — Shard the lockbox.** At 1e6 entries × ~220 B ≈ ~220 MB, a flat lockbox re-publishes hundreds of MB on every append. **Use a HAMT/sharded structure or a generation-delta log** so add-item is O(1) bytes, not O(N).\n\n---\n\n## 3. Concrete metadata schema (field-level)\n\nClean break. Node keys stay **independent random** (no derivation). Read and write are two separate lockboxes with two separate `shareKey`s.\n\n### Node metadata (IPNS-published; unchanged distribution model)\n\n```jsonc\n// FolderMetadata — blob AES-256-GCM under THIS folder's folderKey (unchanged)\n{\n  \"v\": 2,\n  \"entries\": [\n    { \"type\": \"folder\", \"id\": \"...\", \"name\": \"...\", \"ipnsName\": \"k51...child\" },\n    { \"type\": \"file\",   \"id\": \"...\", \"name\": \"...\", \"ipnsName\": \"k51...file\" }\n  ]\n  // NOTE: NO folderKeyEncrypted / fileKeyEncrypted / ipnsPrivateKeyEncrypted here.\n  // Child keys are NOT owner-ECIES-wrapped into the parent blob anymore.\n  // The read-key embedding gap is closed by the lockbox, not by per-entry wraps.\n}\n\n// FileMetadata — CHANGED (correction C1): self-encrypted under the file's OWN fileKey\n{\n  \"v\": 2,\n  \"blob\": \"<AES-256-GCM(fileMeta, fileKey)>\",   // was: under parent folderKey\n  // fileMeta (inside blob): { cid, size, mimeType, fileIv, versions:[...] }\n}\n```\n\nThe owner's authoritative copy of every node's `folderKey`/`fileKey`/`ipnsPrivKey` is held in the owner's vault key store (root key material ECIES-wrapped to owner, as today for the root). Node keys are generated random per node and **never derived from parent or path** — this is what keeps move O(1) and revocation containable.\n\n### Share row (DB — repurposed `shares`, `share_keys` DELETED)\n\n```\nshares {\n  id\n  ipns_name                  -- share-root node (any node: deep folder or single file) — constraint 4\n  recipient_public_key\n  permission                 'read' | 'write'\n  read_lockbox_ipns_name     -- shared across ALL recipients of this share root\n  write_lockbox_ipns_name    -- NULL for read-only shares\n  encrypted_read_share_key   -- ECIES(readShareKey  -> recipient pubkey)   [read chain]\n  encrypted_write_share_key  -- ECIES(writeShareKey -> recipient pubkey) | NULL  [write chain]\n  read_generation  int\n  write_generation int\n  revoked_at       timestamp\n}\n```\n\n### Lockbox objects (own IPNS name + CID; sharer holds the lockbox private key)\n\n```jsonc\n// READ lockbox — sealed under readShareKey\n{\n  \"v\": 1, \"kind\": \"read\", \"generation\": 7, \"root\": \"k51...shareRoot\",\n  \"shards\": [ /* HAMT/sharded — correction C5 */ ],\n  \"entries\": [\n    { \"itemId\": \"k51...A\", \"keyType\": \"folder\",\n      \"sealed\": \"AES-GCM(folderKey_A, readShareKey, AAD='read|k51A|folder|7')\" },  // C3\n    { \"itemId\": \"k51...F\", \"keyType\": \"file\",\n      \"sealed\": \"AES-GCM(fileKey_F, readShareKey, AAD='read|k51F|file|7')\" }\n  ],\n  \"sig\": \"Ed25519(sharer, {generation, root, merkleRoot(entries)})\"            // C4\n}\n\n// WRITE lockbox — sealed under writeShareKey (only referenced by write shares)\n{\n  \"v\": 1, \"kind\": \"write\", \"generation\": 3, \"root\": \"k51...shareRoot\",\n  \"entries\": [\n    { \"itemId\": \"k51...A\", \"keyType\": \"folder-ipns\",\n      \"sealed\": \"AES-GCM(ipnsPrivKey_A, writeShareKey, AAD='write|k51A|folder-ipns|3')\" }\n  ],\n  \"sig\": \"Ed25519(sharer, {generation, root, merkleRoot(entries)})\"\n}\n```\n\n### Read chain vs write chain (separate, per constraint 3)\n\n- **READ chain:** recipient → ECIES-unwrap `encrypted_read_share_key` → `readShareKey` → resolve read-lockbox CID → unseal `{folderKey | fileKey}` per node (AAD-checked) → AES-decrypt `FolderMetadata`/`FileMetadata` (the latter now under its own `fileKey`, C1) → decrypt content. **Never touches any IPNS private key.**\n- **WRITE chain:** recipient → ECIES-unwrap `encrypted_write_share_key` → `writeShareKey` → resolve write-lockbox CID → unseal `ipnsPrivKey` per node → sign/publish IPNS records. A read share carries no `write_lockbox_ipns_name` and no `encrypted_write_share_key`, so write material is never even transmitted on the read path (stronger separation than A's co-located blob).\n\n---\n\n## 4. Flows & Big-O (1e6 items, 10 recipients, balanced depth ≈ 3)\n\n| Operation | Steps | Big-O | Concrete | IPNS republishes |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **share-create** | Build read lockbox: seal each in-scope node key under `readShareKey` (once). ECIES-wrap `readShareKey` to each recipient. (write share: + write lockbox + write key wraps.) | **O(items) seal once + O(recipients) wraps** | 1e6 seals (client CPU) + 10 ECIES wraps, 10 share rows | **1–2** (publish the lockbox object(s)) — node tree untouched |\n| **add-item to shared subtree** | Seal new node key into each covering lockbox; republish that lockbox shard. No per-recipient work. | **O(shards-covering-node)** | 1 seal + 1 shard republish per affected lockbox | **1 per affected lockbox** + the normal 1 parent-folder publish the add already does |\n| **revoke-recipient (cut FUTURE deltas only)** | New `readShareKey'`, re-seal lockbox, bump+sign generation, re-wrap to remaining recipients. | **O(items) re-seal + O(remaining recipients) wraps** | 1e6 re-seals (client) + 9 wraps | **1** (lockbox only) |\n| **revoke-recipient (GENUINE cutoff of existing content)** | Above **plus** rotate every in-scope node's `folderKey`/`fileKey`, re-encrypt each node's metadata/content, re-publish each node's IPNS record, unpin old CIDs; for write: new Ed25519 keypair per node + parent-pointer rewrites (C2). | **O(items) node-rotate + O(items) re-encrypt + O(items) republish + O(items) unpin** | ~1e6 node rotations + ~1e6–2e6 IPNS PUTs | **~1e6** — the irreducible cost, identical in ALL designs |\n| **write→read downgrade** | Drop `write_lockbox_ipns_name` + null `encrypted_write_share_key`. *Future-delta semantics.* True cutoff of a **cached** IPNS key = the C2 Ed25519 rotation storm. | **O(1)** future-delta / **O(items)** if cached-write must be denied | 1 row update | **0** (future-delta) / ~1e6 (cached cutoff) |\n| **move-node** | Node key sealed by stable `itemId`; lockbox entries untouched if still in scope. Re-encrypt moved node metadata under new parent + republish moved node + 2 parents (existing FUSE path). Move-OUT-of-scope = drop entries **and** rotate that node's key (it's a revocation event — orphaned-share fix). | **O(1)** in-scope / **O(node-subtree)** on move-out (rotation) | 2 reseals + republishes (in-scope) | **2** (in-scope) |\n| **recipient navigate-into-deep-child** | Resolve lockbox CID once, ECIES-unwrap `shareKey` once, then O(1) map lookup + unseal per node. | **O(1)** after first fetch | 1 ECIES + N unseals (local) | **0** |\n\n**The two honest realities the table encodes:**\n1. Every *cheap* number assumes **future-delta** revocation semantics (cut new items/generations). 2. Every *genuine* cutoff of already-cached content is **~1e6 IPNS republishes** and is the same in all four designs — it is the cost of forward secrecy against a cached symmetric key, not a property of the share model.\n\n---\n\n## 5. The honest tradeoff\n\n**Gets cheaper (the win):**\n- **share-create:** 2e7 `share_keys` rows → ~10 rows + 1 lockbox object. Eliminates the multi-hundred-MB `childKeys` POST and O(items×recipients) client crypto.\n- **add-item:** O(recipients) `reWrapForRecipients` → O(1) lockbox append. No per-recipient work ever.\n- **write→read downgrade:** O(items) row deletes → O(1) column drop (future-delta).\n- **navigate:** O(depth) DB+ECIES round-trips → one lockbox fetch then all-local.\n- **recipient-facing revoke work:** O(items×recipients) re-wraps → O(remaining recipients).\n\n**Gets more expensive / stays expensive (the cost):**\n- **Genuine revocation and cached-key write-downgrade** are unchanged at ~O(items) IPNS republishes — but this is **not a regression**, because the status quo's \"O(1) revoke\" was unsound (root-key-only rotation). C makes the real cost explicit and strictly cheaper than the DB model on the recipient-facing half.\n- **Lockbox build is O(items) client CPU** at share time (1e6 AES seals) — but it's local CPU, not network, and one-time.\n- **Recipient must fetch a (sharded) lockbox** to navigate — front-loaded bandwidth vs. per-node DB lookups.\n\n**Is the tradeoff acceptable for CipherBox?** **Yes**, given the usage pattern: sharing and growth are frequent; full-subtree revocation of a 1e6-item root is rare and, when it happens, is intrinsically expensive in *any* design. The app already tolerates O(items) IPNS work on bulk operations (it's the TEE/6-hour-republish model). What it cannot tolerate is O(items×recipients) on the *common* path (share/add) — which is exactly what C removes. Pair revocation with a **lazy node-rotation queue** (rotate-on-next-write, accept a bounded window, prioritize the share-root) to spread the republish cost; this is a v1.1 optimization, not load-bearing for correctness.\n\n---\n\n## 6. Downstream blast radius\n\n| Subsystem | Change | Invasiveness |\n|---|---|---|\n| **`packages/crypto`** | Add AAD parameter to `sealAesGcm`/`unsealAesGcm` (C3) **or** standardize per-entry `deriveContextKey` domain-sep; add lockbox sign/verify helpers (C4). HKDF/ECIES/AES/Ed25519 all already present. | **Moderate** — additive, no primitive rewrites |\n| **`packages/core` / metadata schema** | `FileMetadata` self-encrypts under `fileKey` (C1); drop `folderKeyEncrypted`/`fileKeyEncrypted`/`ipnsPrivateKeyEncrypted` from entries; bump schema `v`. | **High** — clean-break schema rework (but no migration; constraint 7) |\n| **`apps/api` shares** | Delete `share_keys` table + `addShareKeys`/`reWrapForRecipients` fan-out; add lockbox-ipns columns + generation; server stores opaque lockbox + ECIES grants only (zero-knowledge preserved). | **High** — core of the rework |\n| **`packages/sdk` share** | Rewrite share-create/add/revoke/downgrade around lockbox build/append/re-seal + ECIES shareKey wrap; navigation reads lockbox not per-node share_keys. | **High** |\n| **`crates/fuse`** | Move path: keep existing reseal; add \"move-out-of-scope ⇒ node-key-rotation\" trigger (orphaned-share fix). Read path: unseal via lockbox. | **Moderate** |\n| **`apps/web`** | Replace `executeLazyRotation` (root-only, unsound) with full subtree-rotation revoke + lockbox re-seal; share UI unchanged semantically. | **Moderate** |\n\n**Top 3 implementation risks:**\n1. **FileMetadata self-encryption (C1) is a deep change** touching upload, versioning (`VersionEntry` per-version `fileKey`), FUSE read, and every `encryptFileMetadata` call site. Highest-surface change; get it right first or single-file shares silently don't work.\n2. **Lockbox sharding + signed monotonic generation (C4/C5)** must be correct against a malicious/rollback server, verified client-side. A partial/mixed-generation lockbox silently 404s some entries — needs explicit tests (flagged in C's review).\n3. **Write revocation Ed25519 rotation cascade (C2)** changes k51 names, rewrites parent pointers, and races IPNS sequence numbers (the project's known stale-sequence 409 / folderTree-desync class). Needs an atomic, sequence-aware rotation batch or it leaves the subtree in a mixed-key state.\n\n---\n\n## 7. Open questions for the maintainer\n\n1. **Revocation semantics — future-delta or genuine cutoff by default?** Is \"revoked recipient can't see *new* items/generations but may retain already-cached content until lazy rotation\" acceptable as the v1 default, with genuine O(items) cutoff as an explicit \"secure-revoke\" action? This single decision determines whether revoke is O(1) or O(items) on the common path.\n2. **Is single-file selective read-revocation in scope?** It's the main justification for the FileMetadata self-encryption rework (C1). If files are *always* shared as part of a folder, you can keep `FileMetadata` under `folderKey` and skip C1 — much smaller blast radius, but you lose per-file granularity.\n3. **Lazy node-rotation queue — build now or defer?** Accepting a bounded post-revoke window (rotate-on-next-write, share-root first) makes revocation operationally viable at 1e6 scale. Is a bounded exposure window acceptable, and is the queue v1 or v1.1?\n4. **Lockbox storage substrate — IPNS object vs. a dedicated server blob store?** C puts the lockbox on IPNS for reuse of existing infra, but it's sharer-owned and recipient-read-only; a plain server-side content-addressed blob (still opaque ciphertext) might be simpler and avoid an extra IPNS keypair per share. Which fits the infra better?\n5. **Write-recipient share-extension:** today write recipients can `addShareKeys`. With a sharer-held lockbox key, only the sharer can append. Is removing multi-writer share-extension acceptable, or must write recipients also be able to append to the lockbox (requires sharing the lockbox write key, weakening C2's revocation story)?"
7	  }

Verified — the claim holds. `executeLazyRotation` (`share.service.ts:602`) generates a new key for **only the share-root folder** (`params.folderIpnsName`), re-wraps that one key for remaining recipients, and the comment at lines 596–598 confirms only that folder's metadata is re-encrypted. **Descendant folder/file keys are never rotated.** So a revoked recipient who cached the subtree keys they were granted keeps reading every descendant by resolving its IPNS name directly. That's a real revocation gap in shipped code, independent of any redesign.

Here's the distilled answer to your question.

## Does metadata-driven make more sense? Partly — but not via chaining

Rework **is** justified, but your chaining instinct (seal child keys under the parent, one root key per recipient) is the wrong axis. The workflow's decisive finding:

> Genuine revocation is **O(items)** node-key rotations + re-encrypts + IPNS republishes in **every** design — you can't claw back a cached symmetric key. That cost is irreducible and identical everywhere.

That one fact reorders everything:

- **Chaining (your A) and HKDF-derivation (B) lose.** Because a child key is reachable from the parent, revoking *one* recipient forces rotating the *entire subtree* → ~1M IPNS republishes on the 2-vCPU/someguy stack. They buy cheap shares at the price of catastrophic revokes.
- **The skeptic's "DB model has cheap O(1) revoke" is false** — precisely because of the bug above. Today's revoke is O(1) *only because it's incomplete/unsound*. A correct DB-model revoke pays the same O(items) storm.
- **The winner is the lockbox (envelope).** One random `shareKey` per share; a single shared lockbox object holds every node key sealed under `shareKey` (built once, reused for all recipients); wrap only `shareKey` per recipient. `share_keys` is **deleted**: 2e7 rows → ~10 rows + 1 object. Node keys stay **independent** (not derived), so revocation is *containable* and write→read downgrade is genuinely O(1).

| | A chaining | B HKDF | **C lockbox** | D minimal |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| share-create | O(recip) | O(recip) | **O(items) once + O(recip)** | needs owner-online |
| add-item | O(1) | O(1) | **O(1) append** | owner-online |
| revoke (real) | O(subtree) ❌ | O(subtree) ❌ | **O(items), recip-facing O(recip)** | same storm, hidden |
| downgrade | unsound | O(subtree) | **O(1)** | cached-key hole |
| move | O(1) | reintroduces O(N×M) | **O(1)** | O(1) |

## The catch (why a *clean break* is what unlocks it)

Today `FileMetadata` is sealed under the **parent folderKey**, so a lockbox sealing only `fileKey` grants nothing — you'd still need the folderKey. The load-bearing schema change is: **make `FileMetadata` self-encrypt under its own `fileKey`**, turning a file into a first-class shareable node (and enabling per-file revocation). Plus four non-negotiable corrections the reviews caught: **write-revoke needs Ed25519 IPNS-keypair rotation** (re-sealing the lockbox does nothing to a cached signing key); **AEAD-AAD-bind each entry** to `itemId|keyType|generation` (else the server transplants sealed blobs between slots); **sign the lockbox + monotonic generation** (else stale-CID rollback); **shard it** (1M entries ≈ 220 MB — can't republish that per append).

## The honest tradeoff

Cheaper on the **common path** (share / add / downgrade / navigate — the O(N×M) blowup is gone). The expensive path (genuine full-subtree revoke ≈ O(items) IPNS republishes) is *unchanged* — but today's "cheap" revoke was unsound anyway, so it's not a regression. Pair with a lazy rotate-on-next-write queue to spread that cost.

> AGENT

You're right, and on the part that matters most to your actual goal. Let me separate where you're right from the two things that genuinely still bite.

**The 2-vCPU point — half right.** Key generation and the re-encryption crypto are client-side, so the staging CPU ceiling is irrelevant there. ✓. But the IPNS *publishes* aren't client-side — every rotated node's new record goes through the API relay → Kubo → someguy (that's the 2-IPNS-PUTs-per-publish path that actually hits the ceiling). So the storm is real server-relayed work. You've said you'll wear that cost, which is a legitimate call — I just want it labeled correctly: it's not free, it's *accepted*.

**The point that flips the recommendation in your favor:** the lockbox the workflow crowned is *itself a sidechain*. It's a per-share object that has to be built, sharded, signed, versioned, and re-synced on every add/move/revoke — the exact "blurry parallel structure that desyncs from the tree" you objected to, just CID-addressed instead of DB-addressed. **True chaining is the only design with no sidechain at all** — the keys live *in* the node metadata, and the DB shrinks to one recipient-wrapped root key per share (a grant, not a shadow copy). So your original instinct serves your stated goal better than the workflow's "winner." The workflow only ranked C above A because it implicitly optimized for *cheap* revocation; once you accept expensive revocation, that advantage evaporates and A's elegance wins.

So I'll confirm: **chaining is viable, and it's the right fit for "all share keys on metadata, no sidechain."** But three things are genuinely hard, and only one of them is the throughput you've already dismissed:

1. **Read/write must be two separate chains.** A read-only recipient gets the read chain (content keys) but must *not* get the IPNS private keys, or they can write. So each node seals two things under two parent keys: its content key (read chain) and its IPNS signing key (write chain). Hand out the read-root for a read share, both roots for a write share.

2. **Write-revocation needs Ed25519 keypair rotation, not just key re-sealing — this is the nasty one.** Rotating folderKeys re-encrypts *content*, but the IPNS *name* (k51) is the hash of the Ed25519 public key. A write-recipient who cached the IPNS *private* key can keep publishing to that name forever, no matter how you rotate content keys. Genuine write-revoke therefore means: new Ed25519 keypair → new k51 name → rewrite the parent's pointer to the child → republish. That cascades up and **races the IPNS sequence-number / folderTree-desync class** you already have scars from (the stale-sequence 409s). This is design work, not a throughput test.

3. **The O(items) rotation must be resumable and idempotent.** Rotating a million nodes is not atomic — if it dies at node 600k, the subtree is half old-key / half new-key, and a revoked recipient still reads the un-rotated half. "Easy to replicate in testing" is true for *throughput*; it is **not** true for *partial-failure recovery*, which is the actual engineering risk. You need a checkpointed, idempotent rotation job (rotate-share-root-first so the entry point is cut even if the tail lags).

None of these kill chaining — they're the spec. And note all three are *uniform* in a chaining world: delete, rename-overwrite, and move-out-of-scope all collapse into one rule — "a node leaving a recipient's scope = rotate that node's key" — which dissolves the whole revocation-gap todo class we've been patching one mutation-path at a time.

My recommendation: commit to **chaining + genuine-cutoff revocation**, and let me run one focused design pass that produces the actual two-chain metadata schema, the share/add/move/revoke flows, and concrete designs for (2) and (3) above — since those are the parts that sink implementations, not the part you've already reasoned through. Want me to kick that off, or keep poking at the model first?

8	## Idea
9	
10	Replace today's coarse, lazy, leak-prone delegation with **eager, scoped, time-boxed,
11	cryptographically-revocable capabilities** — usable for agent↔human and agent↔agent
12	access, and a security upgrade for existing consumer sharing.
13	
14	## Why (the current gap)
15	
16	- **Write-delegation leaks the raw key.** Granting write ECIES-wraps the folder's
17	  **real, un-rotatable Ed25519 IPNS private key** to the recipient (`shared-write.ts`).
18	  Deleting the `share_keys` row does **not** cryptographically revoke it: the holder
19	  can keep signing IPNS records directly and the TEE keeps republishing them. The owner
20	  cannot rotate the IPNS name without re-deriving the folder keypair and re-publishing
21	  the parent.
22	- **Read revocation is lazy + coarse.** `executeLazyRotation` only rotates on the
23	  sharer's *next write* to the folder; there is no TTL/expiry and no scope finer than
24	  the IPNS-folder boundary. A revoked party retains decryption until a future write.
25	
26	For "treat every agent call as hostile," this is a security gap, not a UX nit.
27	
28	## Shape of the work
29	
30	- **Eager rotation on revoke** — rotate the wrapped key immediately, not deferred to
31	  the next write.
32	- **Capability expiry / TTL** — time-boxed grants (TTL on the re-wrapped key / session
33	  key); a possible hook is the existing JWT `scope[]` claim.
34	- **Finer scope** — per-file and read-only grants, op-count caps; below folder level.
35	- **Cryptographic write-revocation** — the core crypto fork: either
36	  (a) **mediated writes** (recipient calls a CipherBox/MCP endpoint that performs the
37	  IPNS publish server-side via the principal's TEE-republish path, gated by a revocable
38	  session — recipient never holds the raw signing key), or
39	  (b) **per-grant rotatable IPNS subkeys** (a delegated folder gets its own ephemeral
40	  IPNS keypair the parent can swap on revoke, time-boxed via the TEE schedule).
41	  Pick one; this is the single biggest design decision and is worth a spike.
42	
43	## Notes / dependencies
44	
45	- Likely touches `METADATA_EVOLUTION_PROTOCOL` (share-metadata schema) and the TEE
46	  republish scheduling.
47	- The ECIES re-wrap-for-a-recipient-pubkey primitive already exists and is the right
48	  base — an agent wallet pubkey is just another recipient node in the share graph.
49	- Closely related: `seeds/blind-share-social-graph.md` (capability-based shares keyed
50	  by IPNS name + CRDT-over-IPNS recipient discovery) and

> AGENT

This is the key addition. The seed crystallizes the **write-revocation fork** my running design doesn't consider — and it points at a better answer than the one I had it pursuing:

- **(a) Mediated writes** — the recipient never holds the raw Ed25519 key; they publish through a relay/MCP endpoint gated by a revocable, TTL'd capability token, and the **TEE signs** (which it already does on the 6h republish path: decrypt-in-hardware, sign, discard). Revoke = invalidate the token — instant, cheap, no rotation cascade.
- **(b) Per-grant rotatable IPNS subkeys** — what my workflow was designing (rotate the keypair on revoke, the expensive Ed25519/sequence-race cascade).

Mediated writes is almost certainly the better fit: it eliminates the nastiest part of my design (the Ed25519 rotation storm racing sequence numbers), gives you TTL and op-caps for free, and rides the TEE trust boundary you already have. It also keeps the no-sidechain goal intact — write *authorization* becomes O(grants) capability tokens in the control plane, while the metadata stays pure read-key chaining. Plus TTL/time-boxing and per-file/read-only scope are now first-class requirements.

That reshapes the schema foundation, so I'll stop the in-flight run and relaunch with this folded in.
